en: The Chapter on Similes, Part One: The Lion Section.
9. The Question on the Snake’s Limbs “Venerable Nāgasena, as for what you said—that ‘three qualities of a snake should be adopted’—which are those three qualities that should be adopted?
“Just as, O Great King, a snake moves by means of its belly;”

In the same way, Great King, a practitioner of yoga should proceed with wisdom. For one proceeding with wisdom, Great King, the mind of the practitioner proceeds according to the principle of knowledge (*ñāya*); it avoids what is contrary in character and cultivates what possesses the correct characteristic.
This, Great King, is the first quality of the snake that should be adopted.
Furthermore, Great King, as the snake moves, it proceeds while avoiding medicinal herbs.
In the same way, Great King, a practitioner of yoga, a follower of the spiritual life, should conduct himself by avoiding misconduct.
This, Great King, is the second quality of the snake that should be adopted.
Furthermore, Great King, when a snake sees people, it becomes distressed, grieves, and reflects.
"In the same way, Great King, when a practitioner of yoga has indulged in evil thoughts and given rise to discontent, he should burn with remorse, grieve, and reflect:
'I have spent this day in negligence; it cannot be recovered again.
This, Great King, is the third quality to be adopted from the snake."
This was also spoken, O Great King, by the Blessed One in the *Bhallāṭiya Jātaka* concerning two *kinnaras*:
"O hunter, we dwelt apart for one night,
Reluctantly, yet mindful of one another."
“Regretting it for even a single night,
we shall grieve, for that night will never come again.
Thus ends the ninth inquiry, the Question on the Serpent.
